title: Quiet on set. How AI transformed China's microdrama scene
content:
Everything seemed to be business as usual as filming got underway on a dimly lit set in a basement in Hengdian, a town nicknamed “China’s Hollywood” for its sprawling complex of film studios.
Cameramen raced around hectically setting up lights and checking shots as choreographers ran through fight sequences and a prop team worked out how to hoist a net that would later restrain a hostage.
Actors, most dressed as assassins and hitmen, milled about or squatted, smoking cigarettes and getting occasional touch-ups from roving hair stylists and make-up artists as they waited for their scene to start.
But behind the bustle was a new reality: while just a few months ago, production of these so-called “microdramas” was flourishing in Hengdian and other hubs – today, these sets are falling quiet.
Seemingly overnight, new AI-video generation tools have taken over the microdrama industry, able to produce these popular, vertical shows at a fraction of the cost, decimating the number of live-action productions across the country and flooding platforms with AI-made content. More than 120,000 microdramas were released in the first three months of this year — with 95% of those generated by AI, according to Chinese state media.
That’s made the industry one of the most visible examples of how China’s breakneck AI transformation is impacting people’s livelihoods — wiping out jobs and creating new ones, leaving everyone unsure what’s next. It’s the kind of technological disruption that many creatives fear could upend movie-making far beyond China.
Between takes actor Junlin, who asked to be identified by her stage name, talks about how she’s struggling to stay afloat as a “bitter winter” has arrived for productions like hers.
“With fewer productions hiring, your space for survival is constantly squeezed,” said the 24-year-old, dressed in combat boots and a high ponytail to play a head assassin who storms around with a posse of hitmen in an upcoming microdrama.
She’d worked only seven days in June, a sharp fall from the spring when she’d been filming 25 out of about 30 days per month in Hengdian and other cities. “I’m someone who gets anxious easily,” she said. “If I’m not on set, I would be in a constant state of anxiety.”
Boom time
Hengdian, a town of just over 200,000 tucked in a rural part of eastern China’s Zhejiang province, had been booming with the rise of the microdrama industry in recent years.
Broken into roughly 90-second episodes, microdramas first emerged during the pandemic, capitalizing on the popularity of short video apps like Douyin and Kuaishou as cinemas and studios closed.
While each episode is designed to be quick to consume on a mobile phone, together the clips weave together plotlines that can stretch the length of a feature film.
These microdramas — and their often soapy or outlandish plots about wicked mother-in-laws, mistaken identities, wartime heroics and wronged lovers — have since proliferated in China and spread to audiences overseas, where they’ve spawned a fast-growing, multi-billion-dollar industry.
They’ve also caught the attention of China’s censors, who are tightening oversight of microdramas with new rules set to take effect in September. Plotlines, for example, will need to “adhere to correct political direction.”
Last year, the domestic microdrama industry was valued at nearly $15 billion, according to market research firm DataEye, almost double the market size for box-office feature films in the country. Its rise ushered in a welcome heyday for young creatives at a time of high youth unemployment in China.
“Once microdramas took off, there was a nonstop stream of roles I could take on as long as I wanted to film,” said Bi Zhiqiang, 27, another actor living in Hengdian, who quickly built a career after moving there in 2021 as the industry was taking shape.
“Many people who didn’t even study acting or film and television joined because there were more and more opportunities.”
The lure drew thousands of crews to Hengdian last year to shoot projects in and around the sprawling Hengdian World Studios.
It was a fresh injection of energy for the town and its decades-old eponymous studio, known for its large-scale replicas of some of China’s iconic imperial architecture, like the Summer Palace and the Forbidden City, and for birthing Chinese blockbusters.
Other hubs — like Qingdao, Xi’an, and Zhengzhou — emerged across the country, too, with microdrama crews shooting in expressly built complexes with fake mansions, boardrooms, and ERs.
But the industry quickly became a pressure cooker for actors and production crews, due to a hyper-competitive model built around cranking out as many microdramas as possible in the hopes that one would go viral.
Actors and crew describe standard 18 to 20-hour working days as productions rushed to stay within budget while shooting what are essentially feature-length movies in the space of roughly a week.
“As long as they keep filming, they can keep releasing. And the logic is — there will always be one that becomes a hit,” said Guo Ertai, a director and actor at the National Theater of China in Beijing, who followed audiences and money into the microdrama industry several years ago.
At the bottom of the pecking order are extras, who might work long shifts for as little as 10 Chinese yuan ($1.50) per hour, a wage one former actor commented wryly was less than the rental rate for some of the animals used in productions.
Even still, the allure of success kept the industry flush with young, ambitious actors, directors and creatives.
Unlike film, which has a high barrier to entry, microdramas “gave an ordinary person an opportunity,” said Guo, the director. The thinking is “‘I can become rich overnight, I can become a star overnight, I can earn a lot of money overnight with very little outlay,’” he said.
Microdrama actors have become celebrities in their own right with millions of followers on social media platforms. Some television and film stars — including martial arts legend Jet Li — have starred in microdramas. Even those without broad name recognition, who were able to land leading roles in successful dramas, could make multiples of an average monthly urban wage.
But as more money and bigger names entered, competition grew fiercer, pushing a drive to export the dramas overseas for more revenue — and use whatever means available to cut costs.
Enter AI
It took a few weeks for actor Zhuang Wenjie, 28, to realize something was wrong when she returned to Hengdian after celebrating the Chinese New Year holiday in her hometown in February.
She had moved to the area last summer and felt she was just beginning to make a name for herself and could start auditioning for higher profile roles.
At first, she didn’t quite connect the empty streets around her with the growing number of AI-generated microdramas she saw on her social media feeds.
Soon, though, it became obvious: people weren’t returning because jobs had dried up. “Suddenly (there was) a feeling of impending crisis,” Zhuang said.
ByteDance’s SeeDance 2.0 had arrived.
Seemingly overnight, Chinese social media was swamped with realistic-looking, AI-generated videos, as users played around with the new, powerful video generation tool.
And when it came to microdramas, SeeDance 2.0 was well positioned. ByteDance owns two of the main platforms in China that host microdramas: Douyin, Tiktok’s sister app, and Hongguo. It also has a repository of novels that make up a well of copyrighted material for scripts that collaborating production teams can draw from.
Other tech firms have released rival video-generating technology in recent months, including another short video app owner Kuaishuo, tech giant Alibaba and AI firm MiniMax.
Using next-gen AI video tools, a 120-minute project of ordinary quality can take a five-member team roughly a week to produce and cost some 15,000 yuan, about $2,200, one production firm told CNN — less than a tenth of what’s typically cite

report.summary: AI视频生成工具冲击中国微短剧行业，95%新剧由AI制作，大量演员失业。
report.background: 微短剧是疫情期间在中国兴起的竖屏短剧形式，每集约90秒，剧情狗血，深受用户欢迎。横店等影视基地曾因微短剧热潮而繁荣，行业估值近150亿美元，吸引大量年轻人入行。然而，2026年字节跳动推出SeeDance 2.0等AI视频生成工具后，制作成本骤降，微短剧行业迅速转向AI生产，导致大量真人剧组停工，演员和幕后人员面临失业危机。
key_points: AI视频工具如SeeDance 2.0能以极低成本生成高质量微短剧，成本仅为传统制作的十分之一。
中国今年前三个月发布的12万部微短剧中，95%由AI生成，真人拍摄项目大幅减少。
横店等影视基地的演员和工作人员收入锐减，例如演员6月仅工作7天，陷入焦虑。
微短剧行业此前竞争激烈，工作时间长、薪酬低，AI的介入进一步挤压了从业者的生存空间。
中国监管部门将收紧微短剧内容审查，要求剧情符合正确政治方向，给行业带来新变数。
report.impact: 对AI行业而言，这展示了生成式视频在内容生产中的颠覆性力量，但也引发版权、就业和伦理争议。对开发者来说，类似工具的开源和商业化机会增多，但需关注技术滥用风险。对普通用户而言，内容供给将极大丰富，但质量参差不齐，且真人影视工作者的生存困境可能影响内容多样性。
report.tools: 可关注字节跳动的SeeDance 2.0、快手（Kuaishou）的视频生成技术、阿里巴巴的AI视频方案，以及MiniMax等公司的相关模型。开源社区可留意Hugging Face上的视频生成模型和工具。
